query: For noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials used in catalysis, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs reliable material formation and the resulting catalytic performance, and why? Specify one controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: When noble metal precursors are reduced under low‐temperature, diffusion‐limited conditions, the inhibition of precursor mobility forces a stochastic, random incorporation of the elements. This promotes the formation of uniform single‐phase HEA nanoparticles that exhibit superior catalytic activity compared to analogous bimetallic systems, due to a more even distribution of active sites.
generation.material_initial_state: A well-mixed solution or solid precipitate of noble metal single-source precursors (both cationic and anionic species) for the intended elements.
generation.intervention: Perform low-temperature reduction under conditions designed to inhibit precursor mobility. Compare a five-element (HEA) precursor mixture with a bimetallic precursor mixture prepared under identical conditions.
generation.conditions: Synthesis is carried out at low temperatures (where the entropy contribution is minor) and under controlled cooling rates that suppress precursor diffusion, similar to the conditions described in PMC10621632. The same concentration and mixing protocols are applied to both multielement and bimetallic samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform atomic mixing at the nanoscale, resulting in single-phase nanoparticles with a random distribution of all constituent metal atoms.
generation.mechanism: At low synthesis temperatures, the reduction process limits the mobility of the individual metal precursors. In a system with five elements, this inhibition of diffusion forces a kinetically driven, stochastic incorporation of the metals into the nucleating particles, preventing phase segregation. In contrast, bimetallic systems, with fewer competing species, are more prone to partial phase separation, which leads to heterogeneous distributions of catalytic sites. The resulting uniformity in HEA nanoparticles enhances catalytic performance via improved synergy among the active sites.
generation.predicted_outcome: The five-element HEA nanoparticles will form as a predominantly single-phase material with a more uniform elemental distribution and will demonstrate higher catalytic performance (e.g., better oxygen reduction reaction efficiency or nitrobenzene hydrogenation yield) than the bimetallic nanoparticles synthesized under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Bimetallic nanoparticles produced under identical low-temperature reduction conditions, which are expected to display partial phase segregation and a less uniform active site distribution, leading to comparatively reduced catalytic performance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for noble metal–based nanoparticles synthesized via low-temperature, solution-based or low-energy reduction methods where precursor mobility is limited. It may not apply under high-temperature or high-diffusivity conditions where entropy-driven stabilization dominates.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported qualitatively by in situ studies and stochastic simulations, the exact quantitative improvement in catalytic performance and the sensitivity of the mechanism to slight variations in precursor concentration or cooling rate remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one using a five-element precursor mixture and the other using a bimetallic mixture. Use identical low-temperature reduction conditions to ensure limited precursor mobility. Characterize both sets using techniques such as in situ X-ray powder diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy to assess phase formation and elemental distribution. Test their catalytic performance via a standard reaction (e.g., oxygen reduction reaction or nitrobenzene hydrogenation) under comparable reaction conditions.
measurements: Phase purity and crystallite uniformity via X-ray powder diffraction
Elemental dispersion and oxidation states via X-ray absorption spectroscopy
Catalytic activity metrics such as conversion rate, yield, and turnover frequency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the five-element HEA does not show a significantly more uniform single-phase structure and improved catalytic performance relative to the bimetallic counterpart, or if both systems display similar degrees of phase segregation and catalytic outputs, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanopartic

reduction of all individual elements (Pt, Ir, Os, Rh, Ru) is followed alongside the crystallization of HEA nanoparticles. Comparing multimetallic precursor mixtures with bimetallic ones, we propose a model for the formation of single-phase nanoparticles. The essential conclusion of the model, i.e., that combining multiple elements favors the formation of single-phase nanoparticles, will aid the design of future studies combining experimental investigations with computational simulations.
## Material synthesis
All samples were prepared following a literature procedure described by Yusenko et al. All compounds were prepared from commercial metal precursors (Sigma Aldrich). As cationic precursors the chloropentaammine metal chlorides of Ir, Rh, and Ru were used; Ir(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, [Rh(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, and [Ru(NH3)5Cl]Cl2. The anionic precursors were the ammonium hexachlorometallates of Ir, Pt, and Os; (NH4)2[IrCl6], (NH4)2[PtCl6], and (NH4)2[OsCl6].
